items.title: docs(rapidata): sync skill docs to SDK v3.19.2
items.body:
Recovers the doc changes that went missing when [run 31594777303](https://github.com/RapidataAI/skills/actions/runs/31594777303) failed.

## Why this is needed

That run's doc-update step failed, but it still committed `chore: sync plugin version to SDK v3.19.2` (6e89e99) — so `plugin.json` and the SKILL.md pin now say **3.19.2** while the docs still describe **3.16.7**. Three releases of API changes were never written up, and because the markers moved, the workflow reports nothing to do ([run 31598253634](https://github.com/RapidataAI/skills/actions/runs/31598253634) went green in 12 seconds without running anything).

This PR writes those changes up, which makes the pin true again. #9 stops the same silent loss from recurring.

## What changed

`+414 / -71` across the three skill files:

- **Audiences** — explicit `start_recruiting()` with a real return value; new `get_recruiting_metrics()` / `RecruitingMetrics` funnel; `create_audience` admission bar (`target_accuracy` / `min_tasks` / `max_tasks`) with defaults and validation errors.
- **Jobs** — non-blocking `get_progress()` / `JobProgress`; `failure_tolerance` on every `create_*_job_definition`; `get_results()` now raising up front when an audience can never produce responses instead of blocking forever.
- **Uploads** — `FailedUploadException.retry()`, `.machine`, `.failures_by_stage`, richer message, new `AssetWarning`.
- **Contexts** — `autoShortenContext` is gone; over-long contexts are always shortened. Batched `shorten_contexts()`.
- **Benchmarks** — `Tag` / `Origin`, `origins` on `add_prompts`, `update_prompt()`, custom leaderboard budgets and prompt-tag scoping.
- **Compare results** — aggregator `4.1.0` result shape.

## Provenance and checking

Generated by the phased pipeline from #7, run against the real `v3.16.7..v3.19.2` SDK diff on a checkout of `main` — the same code path CI would take, so this is also an end-to-end exercise of that pipeline.

Because it is model-generated, I checked the load-bearing claims against the SDK source at `v3.19.2` rather than trusting them:

| Claim | Verified against |
|---|---|
| `start_recruiting(self) -> RapidataAudience` | `audience/rapidata_audience.py:471` |
| `JobProgress{state, completion_percentage, recruiting}` | `job/progress.py:27-29` |
| `failureTolerance` default `0.0` | `config/upload_config.py:166` |
| `autoShortenContext` removed, always-on shortening | `config/upload_config.py` (0 occurrences; `contextShortening` replaces it) |
| `create_audience` defaults `0.75` / `10` + three `ValueError`s | `audience/rapidata_audience_manager.py:24-64` |
| `get_results()` raises only when unrecruitable, not while distilling | `job/rapidata_job.py:121-163` |

All accurate; nothing invented. Still worth a human read on tone and placement — that is the part I cannot verify mechanically.

Depends on nothing, but pairs with #9. Review that one first if you want the guard in place before the content.

items.title: docs: sync benchmark profile budgets with the run-shape matrix
items.body:
## What problem are you trying to solve?

`docs/current/AEGIS_AGENTIC_BENCHMARK_BASELINE.md` states four run-shape values
that contradict the matrix fixture the same section names as their owner.

The section opens with:

> The matrix is the only exact run-shape owner. It defines these profiles:

…and then restates the profile table. Four of those restated numbers are stale
— each one is exactly half of the value currently in
`tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`:

| Value | Baseline doc (lines 199-201, 204) | Matrix fixture (lines 134-191) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `development-pilot` wall budget | 600 seconds | **1200** |
| `standard-held-out` wall budget | 3600 seconds | **7200** |
| `extended-held-out` wall budget | 9000 seconds | **18000** |
| per-attempt timeout | 480 seconds | **960** |

Root cause is traceable to a single commit. `c38a24a6`
(`perf: double agentic benchmark budgets for slow providers`, shipped in
v2.6.9) changed four files:

```
tests/e2e/agentic-benchmark-check.sh
tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json
tests/helpers/test_run_agentic_benchmark.py
tests/helpers/validate_agentic_benchmark_matrix.py
```

The v2.6.9 release note for that change says the three profile definitions
("check 脚本内嵌、校验脚本、fixture 矩阵") were kept in sync. The prose baseline
is a fourth place that also restates those values, and it was not updated.

Concrete impact: the baseline docs are the documented authority read order for
non-trivial work (`AGENTS.md` → `docs/current/README.md` → task-relevant
`docs/current/*.md`). An agent or contributor sizing a benchmark run from this
table plans against half the real ceiling — for `extended-held-out`, 9000s
instead of 18000s. Nothing in the suite compares the prose table against the
matrix, so this drift is silent: the three profile assertions in
`agentic-benchmark-check.sh` pass identically before and after this change
(verified below), because they assert profile presence and policy wording, not
the numeric values.

## What does this PR change?

Updates four stale numbers in `docs/current/AEGIS_AGENTIC_BENCHMARK_BASELINE.md`
to match `tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`. Documentation only
— no code, fixture, test, or behavior change.

## Is this change appropriate for the core library?

Yes. It corrects a `docs/current/` authority document that ships with the
method pack and is part of the documented read order for every user, on every
project type. It is not project-specific, team-specific, or tool-specific, and
it introduces no third-party service or integration.

## What alternatives did you consider?

1. **Remove the numbers from the prose table entirely**, leaving the matrix as
   the sole carrier. Rejected: the section's stated purpose is to describe what
   the matrix defines, and the surrounding prose depends on those figures
   (the wall-clock budget paragraph immediately after explains what the ceiling
   covers). Deleting the table also removes useful reference material, and that
   editorial call belongs to the maintainer, not to an outside contributor.
2. **Extend the automated checks so the prose table is compared against the
   matrix**, which would prevent the next recurrence rather than fixing this
   instance. Rejected *for this PR* because it is a separate, unrelated change
   to the test suite and would bundle two changes into one PR. I am happy to
   open it separately if you want it.
3. **Open an issue instead of a PR.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks for issue-first on
   non-trivial changes; a four-number correction with a traceable root cause is
   trivial enough that a diff is faster to review than a description. Happy to
   convert to an issue if you prefer that ordering.

## Does this PR contain multiple unrelated changes?

No. One file, four lines, one concern: aligning stale restated values with the
fixture that owns them.

## Existing PRs
- [x] I have reviewed all open AND closed PRs for duplicates or prior art
- Related PRs: none found — at the time of writing this repository has no open
  PRs, and no closed-unmerged PRs; the only merged PRs are the maintainer's own.

## Environment tested

| Harness (e.g. Claude Code, Cursor) | Harness version | Model | Model version/ID |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------|-------|------------------|
| Claude Code (used to prepare and verify this change) | 2.1.221 | Claude Opus 5 | `claude-opus-5[1m]` |

Verification commands were run on macOS 26.6 (Darwin 25.6.0), bash 5.x,
Python 3.14.6, against `main` at `fe34c3c` (v2.6.9).

## Evaluation

This is a documentation value correction with no behavior surface, so
before/after eval sessions are not the applicable instrument — there is no
agent behavior to measure, and I did not run any. What I did instead was verify
correctness of the values and prove the change is regression-free against a
stashed baseline:

**1. Value correctness.** Each new number read directly out of
`tests/e2e/fixtures/agentic-benchmark-matrix.json`
(`wallClockBudgetSeconds` = 1200 / 7200 / 18000, `perAttemptTimeoutSeconds`
= 960 on all three profiles), cross-checked against the v2.6.9 release note and
against commit `c38a24a6`.

**2. Scope check — nothing else drifted.** Every other value in the table was
compared to the fixture and matches: repetitions 1/1/3, valid target 2/40/120,
attempt ceiling 2/44/132, workers 2/8/8, preflight 30s, max workers 12. Those
are left untouched.

**3. Repo-wide sweep for other stale copies.** Grepped the whole tree for the
old values; the only occurrences outside this file are in `RELEASE-NOTES.md`,
where they are historical `600→1200` change records and must stay.

**4. Before/after regression proof** (change stashed, re-run, unstashed):

| Check | `main` @ `fe34c3c` | With this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/e2e/agentic-benchmark-check.sh` | 55 pass, 0 fail, exit 1 | 55 pass, 0 fail, exit 1 |
| `tests/e2e/layer1-fast-check.sh --host-profile none` | Passed: 35, Failed: 1 | Passed: 35, Failed: 1 |
| `git diff --check` | clean | clean |

A line-by-line diff of the `[PASS]`/`[FAIL]` output from both `layer1-fast-check`
runs is empty — results are identical item for item.

The single failure in both columns is `agentic benchmark policy`, caused by
`offline Codex fixture platform is unsupported` on macOS. It reproduces on the
unmodified baseline, and it matches what the v2.6.9 release note already records
for this gate ("layer1-fast-check 35/36", the only failure being the
environment-limited offline Codex fixture platform check). It is pre-existing
and unrelated to this change.

## Rigor

- [ ] If this is a skills change: I used `aegis:writing-skills` and
      completed adversarial pressure testing (paste results below)
      — *not applicable: no file under `skills/` is touched.*
- [x] This change was tested adversarially, not just on the happy path
      — *rather than fixing only the discrepancy I first noticed, I diffed
      every value in the table against the fixture (step 2 above), swept the
      whole repo for other stale copies (step 3), and ran the suite on a
      stashed baseline to prove the pre-existing failure was not introduced
      here (step 4).*
- [x] I did not modify carefully-tuned content (Red Flags table,
      rationalizations, "human partner" language) without extensive evals
      showing the change is an improvement
      — *no behavior-shaping prose changed; only four numeric literals.*

## Human review
- [x] A human has reviewed the COMPLETE proposed diff before submission

The complete diff is four lines in one file and was reviewed in full before
submission.

items.title: Re-run gcperfsim-cache benchmark with full-resolution raw capture
items.body:
## Summary

Re-runs the gcperfsim-cache benchmark scenario (Workstation and Server GC) with a fresh full-resolution capture, closing a data gap and refreshing stale peak-pause data.

## Why

gcperfsim-cache was one of three scenarios (along with gcperfsim-churn, gcperfsim-webserver) missing raw per-second dotnet-counters CSV captures under src/ZeroGC/results/raw/ for the Workstation/Server modes -- only the ZeroGC capture existed. Its TimeSeries.PauseTimePct chart series is stride-decimated (~150 points from a ~600-sample capture) by un-benchmarks.ps1, and the un-decimated PauseTimePctStats.Max (11.80% for Workstation) was ~26x higher than the decimated chart's visible max (~0.46%) -- a real, visible contradiction in eport.html between the percentile stats and the "over time" chart for the same run.

## What changed

- Re-ran gcperfsim-cache for Workstation + Server GC, same 600s duration as the rest of the suite, into an isolated output directory (not touching the other 31 runs).
- Merged the two refreshed gcperfsim-cache entries into src/ZeroGC/results/results-full.json, leaving all other runs (including gcperfsim-cache/ZeroGC) untouched.
- Added the previously-missing raw CSVs: src/ZeroGC/results/raw/gcperfsim-cache_workstation.csv, gcperfsim-cache_server.csv.
- Regenerated src/ZeroGC/results/report.html via generate-report.ps1 and synced to docs/zerogc/report.html.

## Note on numbers

The new Workstation capture does not reproduce the prior run's rare one-off pause spike (new Max 0.47% vs old 11.80%). GC pause spikes are inherently stochastic (e.g. a one-off blocking Gen2 collection under memory pressure) -- this is expected run-to-run noise, not a regression. Avg/P50/P90 are consistent with the prior run:

| Stat | Old (Workstation) | New (Workstation) |
|---|---|---|
| Avg | 0.1414% | 0.1195% |
| P50 | 0.1491% | 0.1465% |
| P90 | 0.3536% | 0.3502% |
| Max | 11.80% | 0.47% |

Server mode: Max 2.539% (old) -> 2.139% (new); decimated series max now 0.72% (2.97x understated vs prior ~12.7x-class ratios seen elsewhere), reflecting a smaller and more representative capture.

This does **not** fix the underlying stride-decimation algorithm in Get-Downsampled (un-benchmarks.ps1) -- that remains a separate, known issue. This PR only refreshes the gcperfsim-cache data to close its raw-CSV gap and remove the stale/misleading 118ms-tooltip-vs-4.6ms-chart contradiction for this specific scenario.

Implements `docs/ROADMAP.md` P16 and carries the cross-repo docs sync for this roadmap wave.

**Suite expansion.** Four new categories (`arithmetic`, `state_machine`, `concurrency`, `domain_compliance`) join `dafny_puzzles`/`svcomp_style`: 6 atoms across 2 categories → **84 atoms across 6 categories** in 37 files. Each category pairs verified success cases with counterexample cases carrying a real bug that verification must reject; those are marked both by a `_fail.mm` filename suffix and an `expected: FAIL` header comment.

**Runner semantics.** `run_benchmarks.py` now compares expected against actual instead of counting passes, so `success_rate` generalizes to the expected-outcome match rate and a silently-verifying counterexample fails the suite:

```python
EXPECTED_FAIL_RE = re.compile(r"expected:\s*FAIL", re.IGNORECASE)
result = {"actual": actual, "expected": expected, "matched": actual == expected,
          "escalation_candidates": n, "lean_solver_time_s": None, "lean_status": "SKIP"}
# new aggregate axis: counterexample_catch_rate
```

The producing side of that field lands in mumei-lang/mumei-lean#99.

items.title: benchmarks: derive new vStd proposals from weak categories + cross-project docs sync
items.body:
## Summary

Paper Future Work #11 asked for the benchmark→forge channel to *generate* proposals, not just reorder them. `build_forge_feedback` now emits an optional, backward-compatible field alongside the existing priority bias:

```python
{
    "schema": "mumei.benchmark_forge_feedback/v1",   # unchanged
    ...,
    "generated_proposals": _generated_proposals(categories),  # new, optional
}
```

Old documents without the field keep loading unchanged, and the consumer side (companion `mumei-agent` PR) merges generated proposals only when their target is not already covered by gap analysis, so nothing existing is displaced.

Generation is signal-gated and deterministic — a category only produces proposals when a weakness signal crosses `PROPOSAL_WEAKNESS_THRESHOLD`, and each signal maps to a fixed atom template:

| signal | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `expected_outcome_mismatch` | the category's expected-outcome match rate is low |
| `counterexample_missed` | bug-catching cases were not rejected as expected |
| `trusted_atoms_present` | the stdlib domain still leans on trusted atoms |

Solver-time pressure deliberately stays a *priority-only* signal: slow obligations say nothing about missing coverage, so they must not fabricate atoms. Proposal names/targets derive from the category's stdlib domain (`std/math` → `std/math/benchmark_gaps.mm`), and proposals are ordered by weakness score, so re-running the suite on identical results yields byte-identical output.

Docs are synced in the same diff (canonical roadmap reviewed alongside, no competing priority order or alias):
- `docs/CROSS_PROJECT_ROADMAP.md`: new rows for the widened Lean tactic ladder + learned ordering and for conservative ambiguity reporting; live generated theorem paths 12 → 13

## Change Summary

This PR adds comprehensive benchmarking infrastructure and documentation for optimizing dual sync/async client generation and migrating to SQLAlchemy:

### Benchmarking Suite (`benchmarks/pg-lab/`)
- **`schema_gen.py`**: Generates a realistic 45-model publishing platform schema (organizations, teams, sites, posts, comments, billing, webhooks, etc.) with mixed 1-1/1-N/N-M relations, self-relations, enums, and complex types. Parameterized to support different generator options for optimization testing.
- **`optimize_loop.py`**: Autonomous optimization loop that iteratively tests candidate generator options against a live PostgreSQL database, accepting changes only if they improve composite cost (memory × import × connect × query latency) by ≥0.5% without regressing query latency.
- **`workload.py`**: Measurement harness that imports both sync and async clients, connects to PostgreSQL, and runs a mixed query workload (find_many with includes, find_unique, count, create/delete, query_raw) to measure real-world performance.
- **`dual_interface.py`**: Existing benchmark enhanced to measure the cost of generating clients twice (sync + async) vs. a unified package prototype that shares models/types/bases.
- **`lab.sh`**: Database setup script supporting both Docker Compose and system PostgreSQL fallback.
- **`docker-compose.yml`**: PostgreSQL 16 container configuration for benchmarking.
- **`seed.sql`**: Idempotent seed data for consistent workload measurements.
- **`results-2026-08-03.json`**: Example optimization loop results showing 66% composite cost reduction through recursive types, minimal runtime, unified packaging, and separate model files.
- **`README.md`**: Documentation of the pg-lab harness, candidate ladder, and usage instructions.

### Documentation
- **`docs/migrating-to-sqlalchemy.md`**: Migration guide for applications moving from Prisma Client Python to SQLAlchemy, leveraging existing seams (schema as data, client indirection, plain Pydantic models, raw SQL support) for incremental, reversible migration.
- **`docs/contributing/unified-sync-async-client.md`**: Design analysis and proposal for unifying sync and async client generation into a single package, with measured impact showing 99% reduction in marginal memory cost of the second interface (42 MB → 0.3 MB at 20 models, 218 MB → 2.3 MB at 50 models).

The benchmarking suite enables data-driven optimization of the generator for applications using both sync and async interfaces simultaneously. items.title: fix(ci): #4211 — sync the conformance docs AFTER the high-water raise, not before
items.body:
The recurring `quality` failure that has blocked every open PR three times today, traced to its cause rather than patched again.

## Symptom

```
[sync-conformance] DIFFERS  README.md (standalone)
  committed: **standalone (host-free) test262 conformance**: 28,257 / 43,505 (65.0 %)
  generated: **standalone (host-free) test262 conformance**: 28,270 / 43,505 (65.0 %)
```

The mismatch is between **main's own README** and **main's own committed artifacts** — nothing to do with the PR being tested. It clears only when some unrelated PR happens to carry a `sync:conformance` commit, and returns on the next baseline bump.

Seen three times on 2026-08-07 (28,222→28,227, then 28,257→28,270), and it parked **nine PRs** that morning. #4178 repaired that instance without finding the cause.

## Root cause

`sync-conformance-numbers.mjs` derives **two** numbers from **two different files**:

| line | source |
|---|---|
| JS-host conformance | `benchmarks/results/test262-current.json` |
| **standalone (host-free)** | **`benchmarks/results/test262-standalone-highwater.json`** |

In `baseline-summary-sync.yml` the order was:

1. copy the fresh `test262-current.json`
2. **run `sync-conformance-numbers.mjs`** ← reads the *old* high-water mark
3. **`check-standalone-highwater.mjs --update`** ← raises the mark
4. `git add` the mark **and** the README, and commit

So one commit carries a **new mark** and a README synced from the **old** one. Not a race, not flaky — a deterministic inconsistency emitted **every time the mark rises**.

The `promote-baseline` job in `test262-sharded.yml` carries a comment insisting this sync "must update everything derived from it ATOMICALLY in the same commit". That intent was right; this job silently broke it, because the standalone half derives from an artifact written *later in the same job*.

The **re-anchor / retry path** had the same defect in subtler form: it re-applies the snapshotted README — already synced against the *original* mark — then recomputes the mark against main's freshly fetched tip (`max(ours, main's)`), and never re-syncs.

## Fix

- **Fresh path** — the sync now runs *after* the raise, when both inputs are final.
- **Re-anchor path** — re-run the sync after the recompute, and re-stage `README.md ROADMAP.md CLAUDE.md plan/goals/goal-graph.md`.

`refresh-baseline.yml` already had the correct order (raise ~447, sync ~780) and is **unchanged**. `test262-sharded.yml`'s promote job syncs from an artifact that is already final and is **unchanged**.

## Why chase it instead of patching again

The per-PR repair is one line and takes a minute, which is exactly why it kept being the chosen response. The minute is not the cost:

- it blocks **every** open PR at once, so it scales with queue depth;
- the failure names the **PR's own** `quality` job, so each lane diagnoses it from scratch as though it were their own regression — three lanes did that today;
- it recurs on every baseline bump, several times a day.

## Verification

`baseline-summary-sync.yml` parses (`yaml.safe_load`), and both `sync` calls now follow their corresponding raise — verified by line order: raise 224 → sync 237, raise 333 → sync 343.

**The real proof is behavioural and arrives on the next high-water rise:** main should stay self-consistent and no PR should need a hand-carried sync commit. If one does, this fix is incomplete and there is a third writer — stated in the issue file so the next person isn't misled by a green CI run here.

items.body:
## Summary

This PR closes all open Phase 3 issues (#8, #9, #10, #12, #13, #14) on the
`feature/p3-ml-workload-parity` branch and brings the MPI multi-driver
architecture to a fully validated state before Phase 4 Docker containerisation.

---

## Issues Closed

| Issue | Title | Status |
|---|---|---|
| #8 | Broadcast seed centroids from rank 0 before K-Means iteration loop | ✅ Fixed |
| #9 | Broadcast global mean/std from rank 0 for consistent LogReg feature standardisation | ✅ Fixed |
| #10 | Validate data integrity: MPI multi-driver vs single-driver Spark baseline | ✅ Passing |
| #12 | Benchmark sync overhead: MPI multi-driver vs single-driver baseline | ✅ Done |
| #13 | Update requirements.txt and README for mpi4py + OpenMPI (Phase 3) | ✅ Done |
| #14 | WordCount regression test: MPI multi-driver result matches baseline | ✅ Done |

---

## What Changed

### Correctness fixes (Issues #8 & #9)
- **K-Means (#8):** `allreduce.py` — rank 0 now calls `init_centroids()` on its
  local partition and `comm.Bcast` the result to all ranks before the iteration
  barrier. All ranks start iteration 1 from the **same** K centroid positions,
  making convergence reproducible across runs.
- **LogReg (#9):** `local_gradient.py` — introduced `_broadcast_global_stats()`:
  rank 0 computes global `mean` and `std` over the full dataset in a single Spark
  pass, then `comm.Bcast` both arrays to all ranks. All ranks standardise their
  features identically, matching MLlib's internal `StandardScaler` and eliminating
  the gradient-space mismatch.

### Parity validation fixes (Issue #10)
- Replaced invalid centroid L2 delta (partition-dependent) with **WCSS relative
  delta ≤ 1%** — the standard Lloyd (1982) criterion.
- Replaced invalid weight-vector L2 delta (L-BFGS vs SGD comparison) with
  **accuracy delta ≤ 3pp** on a shared 1000-row evaluation sample.
- Removed meaningless intercept delta check (MLlib real intercept vs MPI
  bias-in-weights intercept=0).
- Fixed `--metrics-dir` plumbing so metrics CSVs are actually written to
  `./metrics/` and consumed by `timing_analysis.py`.

### Instrumentation & analysis
- **`scripts/timing_analysis.py`** — timing decomposition into Spark time vs sync
  time per iteration; derives `spark_fraction`, `sync_overhead_pct`, rank
  variance, and bottleneck mode. Writes `controller_feature_matrix.csv` — the
  Objective 2b LSTM/regression input.
- **`scripts/sync_overhead_benchmark.py`** — runs single-driver baseline + reads
  MPI metrics CSVs; writes `results/sync_overhead_benchmark.csv` for Objective 2d
  evaluation (closes #12).

### Docs & dependency (Issue #13)
- `requirements.txt`: `mpi4py>=3.1` with OS-level OpenMPI note.
- `README.md`: Phase 3 Prerequisites (Ubuntu/macOS/Docker),
  `generate_datasets.py` one-time setup, all `mpirun -n 5` commands, sync
  benchmark usage, Queue deprecation note.

### Regression test (Issue #14)
- `tests/phase3/test_wordcount_mpi_vs_baseline.py` — two tests guarded with
  `@pytest.mark.skipif(mpi_size < 2)`: `test_top_n_counts_match` and
  `test_all_words_present_in_mpi_output`. A `test_skipped_in_single_rank`
  smoke-test ensures CI stays green.
- Added missing `tests/phase3/__init__.py` and `tests/logreg/__init__.py` —
  fixes `pytest tests/ -v` collection errors.

---

## Parity Results (N=5, 540 K rows)

| Metric | Value | Tolerance | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| K-Means WCSS relative delta | 0.89% | ≤ 1% | ✅ PASS |
| LogReg accuracy delta | < 2pp | ≤ 3pp | ✅ PASS |
| DATA INTEGRITY CHECK | — | — | ✅ CONFIRMED |

## Timing Analysis (N=5, 540 K rows)

| Workload | Bottleneck | Spark fraction | Sync overhead | Iterations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K-Means | compute | 0.963 | 3.74% | 4 (converged) |
| LogReg | sync | 0.375 | 62.51% | 14 (not converged) |

> K-Means: allocate more `cores_per_worker`.
> LogReg: tune MPI transport (UCX) or increase learning rate.

---

## Test Results

- All `tests/unit/` tests: pass without MPI
- All `tests/phase3/` MPI-guarded tests: skip cleanly in CI
- `tests/logreg/`: pass without MPI

---

## Next Phase

After this PR merges to `dev`, the next work item is **Phase 4 — Docker
containerisation**:
- One container per MPI rank, NFS-backed shared Docker volume
- OpenMPI inside containers, `mpirun` across container network
- Validate at scale on Docker Swarm (2–3 physical nodes)

Objective 2 (resource allocator) work begins in parallel on a new feature branch
once the `controller_feature_matrix.csv` dataset is expanded (vary `k`,
dataset size, `num_ranks`).

## Summary

Two research deliverables for the issues assigned to me.

Closes #187. Addresses #99 as far as it can go while #100 is open.

## #187 — `docs/research/encrypted-byo-storage-sync.md`

Compares local export, filesystem/NAS targets, generic S3-compatible storage, and consumer drive providers on privacy, portability, cost, offline behaviour, and maintenance. Recommends a v1 boundary of **manual, encrypted, resumable snapshots to an S3-compatible endpoint or a filesystem path**, behind a `SyncTarget` interface kept deliberately separate from the live `StorageBackend`.

Two findings from the code shaped the design:

- The provider-neutral storage abstraction **has already landed** (`storage_abstract.py`, `storage_factory.py`, …), so the ADR's "not started" status line is stale.
- **The vault no longer encrypts media at rest.** Per the vault design note, 1.1.3 keeps hidden media in the ordinary private store behind password-gated sessions and migrates legacy AES-GCM blobs back to plaintext. It is an access-control boundary, not a cryptographic one — so the requirement that "vault blobs are encrypted locally before upload" **cannot be met by reusing vault behaviour**. Sync must own its own encryption layer.

Consumer drive providers are deferred with reasons: OAuth puts a Find-registered client identity in the trust path, which weakens the local-first promise beyond the engineering cost. Users wanting Drive/Dropbox can point the filesystem target at a provider-synced folder or an `rclone mount` — covers the case in v1 with zero provider code.

items.title: Prefix skill names, gate ara/ and Hard Rule 7, add review skill
items.body:
Closes five gaps found in an agentic-workflow review across this repo, `structsplat`, and `IntrinsicEngine`. Companion PRs exist in the other two.

## 1. Skill names collided across repositories

`verify`, `bench`, `docs-sync`, and `experiment` are generic enough that a sibling repository open in the same agent session shadows them. This was **observed live**: in a multi-repo session this repo's `docs-sync` skill won and structsplat's became unavailable to the agent entirely.

All four are renamed `rtgs-*`, joining `realtime-gs-results-audit` which already was prefixed. `.agents/skills/` now mirrors all six rather than one. A new test asserts every skill name is repo-prefixed and matches its directory name, so an unprefixed skill cannot be added back silently.

## 2. `ara/` was invisible to agents

The claim ledger holds 24 claims and is actively committed, but `ara/` appeared **zero times** in `CLAUDE.md` — it was referenced only from inside the results-audit skill. An agent that never loaded that skill could put a number in `README.md` without touching the ledger.

- New "Evidence and claims" section in `CLAUDE.md`: layout, the nine claim fields, the status vocabulary, and the `Boundary` convention.
- New `scripts/check_ara.py`: required layer files, `PAPER.md` index targets, claim-field completeness, status words, dependency resolution, proof-path existence, staging-ID resolution.
- New Hard Rule 8 stating the requirement at contract level.

`runs/` is deliberately excluded from proof-path checking because it is gitignored — a fresh clone cannot resolve it, so a durable binding must be a tracked path.

## 3. Hard Rule 7 was unenforceable prose

Rule 7 mandates a calibrated `dataset/` run, saved PLYs, previews, a summary-bound relative-link `index.html`, and smoke receipts for both that page and an `rtgs view` command. Neither `verify.sh` nor `docs_sync.py` mentioned `index.html`, `viewer`, or `dataset` — the strictest requirement in the repo had the weakest enforcement.

New `scripts/check_results_bundle.py` checks:

- the artifacts and previews `rtgs run --out [--preview]` actually writes
- `metrics.json` parses, has a non-empty `metrics` object, and carries no non-finite values
- `index.html` exists, uses relative links, and every local target resolves
- the page carries the summary numbers rather than only linking `metrics.json`
- a receipt records both the page smoke test and the exact `rtgs view` command

`--no-previews` covers a legitimately preview-free run. Rule 7 now names the gate.

## 4. No review skill

Adds `rtgs-review`: the five hard-rule gates, a gradient-safety and numerical-stability pass for differentiable code, and a claim-hygiene step that asks whether prose overstates its artifact — the thing `check_ara.py` structurally cannot judge.

## 5. `scripts/` had no lifecycle policy

New `scripts/check_script_layout.py` requires every top-level `scripts/` file to be declared durable with a reason, and documents `scripts/experiments/` as the destination for new one-off drivers.

**The two `iter1e` scripts are allowlisted as PINNED rather than moved.** Their paths are bound by source hash in `DECLARED_SOURCE_PATHS` in `benchmarks/inverse_projection_fiber_iter1e.py` and cited by sealed notes under `benchmarks/results/`. Relocating them would break replay integrity of committed evidence, which `realtime-gs-results-audit` forbids. The policy applies to new scripts; existing sealed provenance is not rewritten to satisfy a layout rule.

## Bidirectional docs check

`docs_sync.py` gains a reachability check in the opposite direction from its existing path check: every `docs/*.md` must be nameable from `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, or `AGENTS.md`, transitively through other reachable docs.

It found `docs/DESIGN_field_lift.md` reachable only from `ara/logic/solution/`, never from an entrypoint. The `CLAUDE.md` repository map now covers it, plus `ara/` and `dataset/`, which the map omitted entirely.

## Verification

- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`: clean.
- `docs_sync`, `check_ara` (24 claims), `check_script_layout` (9 durable scripts): OK.

items.title: feat(du): Disk usage utility with clonefile checks
items.body:
## What

Correctness work on `tools du`, the APFS-aware disk usage scanner.

- **Reports denials** instead of silently under-counting directories it could not read.
- **Allocated bytes, sparse files and clone partners** are reported distinctly, and extent maps are cached so the same inode is not re-mapped per link.
- **Detects blocks shared outside the scan root** and leads with *freeable* bytes — the number that actually answers "how much space do I get back if I delete this", which differs sharply from apparent size once clones are involved.
- **Stops the walk at filesystem and cloud-provider boundaries**, so a scan no longer wanders into a mounted volume or a cloud-synced placeholder tree.
- Docs: corrected the huge-directory note and dropped identifying paths from the benchmark log.

## Why

`du` lies on APFS. A tree of bun `node_modules` cloned across worktrees reports its full apparent size N times over, so the number that looks like "reclaim 40 GB" is often "reclaim 4 GB". Leading with freeable bytes makes the output actionable.

## Performance

The native core (`src/du/native/clonesize.c`) is syscall-bound and runs in the hot loop of multi-million-file scans, so per repo convention every feature here is measured and recorded in `.claude/docs/benchmarks-du.md`.

## Scope

`src/du/**`, `src/utils/format.ts` (+ its test), `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/docs/benchmarks-du.md`.

items.title: docs(benchmarks): i7-12700K result pages with figures and fresh measurement data
items.body:
Closes #320.

## What this adds

The benchmark results site, in the shape #320 asked for:

- **`docs/benchmarks/systems.md`** — landing page indexing the machines. Full topology, all six vendor library versions, the pinning policy and *why* it is mandatory on a hybrid P/E-core CPU, and an "adding a system" procedure.
- **`docs/benchmarks/i7-12700k.md`** — the full result page: four figures, tables, and a written assessment for every suite.
- **Four figures** in `docs/img/benchmarks/`, regenerated from the committed CSVs with the existing `plot_results.py` / `analyze_scaling.py` tooling.

Adding a second machine costs one new page and one table row — no existing page needs editing.

## Measurement

One session on a quiet i7-12700K. Every backend was verified to link what its label claims *before* measuring (`native` resolves no external BLAS, `openblas` → `libopenblas.so.0`, `blis` → `libblis.so.4`, `mkl` → the `libmkl_*` trio), so no curve is silently the generic path wearing a vendor label.

Covered: 5 BLAS backends, 3 LAPACK backends, 4 GEMM-scaling backends, 5 #297 kernel families, and both sparse scoreboards — 20 CSVs.

The previous committed CSVs predated #227 and covered only `dot`/`nrm2`/`gemv`/`gemm`. This run covers the full L1/L2/L3 core (15 ops) and adds **BLIS, which had never been measured at all**.

## Findings

**The #82 GEMM gate now fails.** 76.3% of OpenBLAS at N=465, against 80.2–86.5% at every other size. I re-ran N=465 three times in isolation — 70.6%, 75.4%, 72.5% — so this is a reproducible localized dip, not noise, and it contradicts the previously documented "80–84% for all N ≥ 256". It looks like a tiling interaction at that specific size rather than a broad regression; worth its own investigation.

**Multi-core GEMM scaling improved** — native-fast reaches 6.51× on 8 P-cores (previously 5.82×), narrowing the 8-thread gap to OpenBLAS from ~62% to ~70%.

**Native LU trails SuperLU by 2–18×, tracking fill monotonically.** Native wins on `add32` (3.3× faster, half the fill) and loses 18× on `bbmat`, where it produces 2.49× SuperLU's fill. It loses twice over on dense-fill problems: more arithmetic, done with scalar non-supernodal kernels. Residuals stay sound (1.1e-15 to 2.2e-14), so these are performance comparisons, not accuracy trade-offs.

**MKL is 3.5× slower than BLIS at small N** (17.5 vs 59.9 GFLOP/s at N=65) and only leads from N ≈ 305.

**Sparse triangular solves do not scale** in any structure — best 1.13× (arrow), worst 0.87×. This *reproduces* the existing #297 result (1.06× / 0.87×) rather than contradicting it.

## Also in this PR

- Measured numbers move out of `benchmarks/README.md` onto the result page, so a re-run updates them in one place. The README keeps the how-to and links out.
- `sync-content.mjs`: `FILE_MAP` entries are now also registered under a `../docs/` key, so a repo-root file (`benchmarks/README.md`, synced via `ROOT_FILE_MAP`) can link into `docs/` with a path that is correct on GitHub *and* rewritten for the site. Without this the README's links to the result page would render as dead relative links.

## Verification

`npm run build` — 43 pages (was 41). All four figures resolve to `/mtl5/img/benchmarks/*.png`, cross-links resolve in both directions (`/mtl5/benchmarks/`, `/mtl5/benchmarks/systems/`, `/mtl5/benchmarks/i7-12700k/`, `/mtl5/design/issue-297-threading-results/`).

## Caveats stated on the page

The CPU governor was `powersave`, so clocks are not pinned; the FMA-peak percentages inherit a ~78 GFLOP/s estimate; and absolute GFLOP/s depend on measurement protocol (a short single-size process reports materially lower numbers than the same size inside a warm sweep). The #297 sparse family ran at grid sides `100,160` rather than the driver default, which does not complete on this machine — see #321 and #322.

- `docs/batch-drift-regression.md` - adds a `Result freshness` section documenting both `exit 3` conditions and the new override, qualifies the Outputs row so committed strategy results are not read as grading candidates, and refreshes `last_reviewed`.
- `docs/deep-audit-2026-05-29.md` - the reconciliation row for `batch-drift-regression-stale-result-pass` moves from Open to Resolved. The finding body is not edited.
- `CHANGELOG.md` - Unreleased/Fixed entry.
- `docs/.index/manifest.yaml` - re-synced for the three edited documents.

## Rationale

The failure mode this closes is worse than a missing gate. `run-regression.sh` selected its grading input with `ls -t "$RESULTS_DIR"/${STRATEGY}-*.json | head -1` and applied no freshness check, while a non-zero benchmark exit was downgraded to a warning. Two matching result files are git-tracked and satisfy that glob. So a benchmark that failed before writing any output still produced a full threshold assertion against a file committed in April, and the nightly job reported success having measured nothing from that run.

A gate that cannot fail reads identically to a gate that passes. The rest of the `tests-ci` cluster was hardened specifically to remove that class of false confidence, which is why this one finding was worth closing rather than deferring.

The partial mitigation already in the workflow does not reach this path: `Fail job on threshold breach` is gated on `steps.regression.outcome == 'failure'`, and the stale-file route produces a genuine `passed: true`, not a failure outcome.

## Scope

Two points where this deviates from the issue text, both deliberate.

**The committed result files are retained, not deleted or gitignored.** The issue proposes removing them so nothing can satisfy the glob. They are not test fixtures: `docs/tier2-benchmark-results.md` cites both as the 5-item baseline and 30-item benchmark evidence, and `docs/batch-drift-regression.md` classifies strategy results as `Permanent (committed)`. Deleting them would remove the evidence those documents rest on. Acceptance criterion 3 admits the alternative - "or the selection is timestamp-guarded so that it cannot" - so the guard does the work and the evidence stays.

**The workflow is unchanged.** `continue-on-error: true` remains on the regression step. The new `exit 3` paths surface as `steps.regression.outcome == 'failure'`, which the existing `Fail job on threshold breach` step already converts into a job failure. Widening the workflow was not needed to satisfy any acceptance criterion.

Implementation notes a reviewer may want to weigh:

- Freshness is anchored on a `mktemp` marker compared with `find -newer` rather than on parsed timestamps. `stat` format flags differ between GNU and BSD; `-newer` does not, so this holds on the macOS leg.
- A one-second sleep separates the marker from the benchmark invocation. On filesystems with whole-second timestamp granularity, a marker and a result file written in the same second would make strict `-newer` reject a genuinely fresh result. Against a benchmark measured in hours this is free, and `touch -d '1 second ago'` was rejected as GNU-only.
- `run-benchmark.sh --reset` still does not clear `RESULTS_DIR`, which the issue notes. The timestamp guard makes that harmless, so it is left alone.

**The audit row is updated in place rather than given a new dated section.** The maintenance model the document declares protects *finding bodies*, not the reconciliation log, and the log's `Closed by` column exists precisely to be filled. Leaving the row as written would be worse than silence: it asserts the finding is "unchanged at every line number the finding cites", which this PR makes false, in the section the document names as its authoritative status source. A new dated section was rejected on two counts - the existing section is already dated 2026-07-20, so a second one would duplicate the heading, and adding a section shifts every finding heading below it, forcing a manifest rewrite that would collide with #857. Line 591 is untouched.

The operations guide needed the opposite treatment. It contained nothing false about result selection because it documented result selection at all - no exit-code table, no selection rule, no environment list. That absence is why the first pass read as clean. With two new `exit 3` paths and a new override, an operator hitting `exit 3` on the nightly job would have had nowhere in the docs to look, so the gap is filled rather than left for the next reader to reverse-engineer from the script.

## Verification

- `tests/batch_drift_regression/test-run-regression.sh`: 44 passed, 0 failed (35 before this change, so all pre-existing assertions still hold).
- `tests/batch_drift_benchmark/test-run-benchmark.sh`: 31 passed, 0 failed. Sibling suites (extractors, aggregate-results, seed-scratch-repo): 3/3 pass.
- `tests/scripts/test-ci-wiring.sh`: 44 passed, 0 failed. `tests/scripts/test-nonstandard-test-wiring.sh`: 80 passed, 0 failed - no new test file, so the registry needed no entry.
- `scripts/validate-doc-index.sh`: `OK (269 documents)`. The count is unchanged from before the edit, confirming entries were updated rather than added or dropped.
- `bash -n` on both modified scripts: clean. Zero CR bytes in all five changed files, so the recorded byte sizes hold on a fresh Linux checkout.

The new tests were checked for vacuity by reverting the production logic and re-running: 6 of the 9 new assertions fail under the old code, and the two "does not report pass" cases reproduce the original defect exactly, printing `REGRESSION TEST PASSED` while grading a backdated fixture. The normal-grading case passes under both old and new logic, which rules out a guard that simply rejects everything.

## Risks

- The guard's granularity assumption is the one thing that could bite. If a filesystem reported timestamps coarser than one second, the sleep would no longer guarantee separation and a fresh result could be rejected - a false failure, not a false pass, so it fails safe.
- A successful run still overwrites `tests/batch_drift_regression/last-run-summary.json`, which is anchored on the regression directory and therefore not redirected by `BATCH_DRIFT_BENCHMARK_DIR`. The file is gitignored and documented as retained only until the next run, so tests overwriting it is harmless; this is noted in the test file rather than worked around.
- `BATCH_DRIFT_BENCHMARK_DIR` is a test seam in a production script. It defaults to the current path and is documented in the script header as test-only, but it is a new way to point the regression at an arbitrary directory.

## Follow-up Work

None opened by this PR. The remaining reconciliation work in the audit document is already tracked: #857 covers the `hooks-parity`, `settings-schema`, and `hooks-correctness` clusters as one unit, and #856 covers the two `sensitive-file-guard.ps1` parity gaps the audit never recorded. With this change the `tests-ci` cluster has no open findings left; every other cluster still reads as of 2026-05-29.

One merge-order note for whoever picks up #857. Both PRs touch `docs/deep-audit-2026-05-29.md` and `docs/.index/manifest.yaml`, so a textual conflict in the manifest is expected. There is no scope overlap - #857 explicitly excludes `tests-ci`, and this PR touches only the `tests-ci` row - but merging this one first is cheaper: it changes a single `size` field in the deep-audit manifest entry, whereas #857 adds a dated section and must recompute section line numbers regardless. In the reverse order, this PR would have to re-verify those line numbers on top of its own change.

Closes #855

items.title: feat(benchmarks): P16-C forge feedback producer + roadmap/paper sync
items.body:
## Summary

Closes the last Planned item of P16 (paper Future Work #12): the benchmark suite now *feeds* the vStd forge / proliferate pipeline instead of only reporting into `docs/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md`.

`run_benchmarks.py --forge-feedback <path>` scores each category and writes a `mumei.benchmark_forge_feedback/v1` document:

```python
weakness = 0.5 * (1 - success_rate)                    # expected-outcome match
         + 0.3 * (1 - counterexample_catch_rate)       # missed bug-catching
         + 0.2 * trusted_ratio                         # unproven atoms
priority_delta = -round(weakness * MAX_PRIORITY_BOOST)  # lower priority runs earlier
```

plus non-scoring `signals` (`z3_solver_time_pressure`, `lean_escalation_cost`, …) and the `CATEGORY_STD_DOMAINS` mapping from benchmark category to stdlib domain (e.g. `arithmetic -> ["std/math", "std/algebra"]`). The delta is negative on purpose: the forge queue treats lower `priority` as earlier execution, so a weak category pulls its domains forward. When a domain is claimed by several categories the strongest bias wins, and a perfect suite yields all-zero deltas (which is what the current suite produces — verified by a real run).

items.body:
## Intent

Implement Megamind Phase 4 evaluation on top of the landed Phase 3 release. Ship two deterministic, provider-neutral, network-free evaluation surfaces: a frozen, synthetic, mixed-language-safe release benchmark exercising the real public CLI across exact, near, paraphrase, ambiguous, no-match, privacy routing, model-access enforcement, privacy canaries, context-budget accounting, deterministic repeatability, and honest local baselines; and an isolated three-arm contract for identical pre-authored tasks under no-wiki, current-wiki, and updated-wiki conditions. Freeze versioned task sets, prompts, model/provider identifier, tools, effort, rubric, thresholds, seeds, and all other inputs; isolate sessions, caches, writable roots, and arm outputs; blind labels; account for authorized context actually supplied; reject cross-arm contamination, missing provenance, post-hoc threshold changes, and malformed results. Megamind plans, validates, scores, and records but never invokes a model, worker, network, account, or external service. Promotion requires improved target outcomes, no material adjacent regression, preserved provenance, zero new privacy/model-access violations, and preregistered thresholds. Failed or incomplete results are typed rollback-required or unsettled; provisional wikis remain untrusted until a full pass. Append safe audit events without prompt, canary, secret, or sensitive leakage. Preserve all Phase 1-3 contracts and add versioned schemas, commands, fixtures, thresholds, ADR/architecture/roadmap/skill docs, migration notes, tests, and bounded offline CI benchmark. No pilots, fleet rollout, remote publication, account changes, worker dispatch, spending, or external research.

## What Changed

- Adds `bench run|check` (`src/megamind/evaluation.py`, `src/megamind/cli.py`): a frozen, network-free release benchmark that drives the real public CLI over a synthetic mixed-language fixture (`evals/fixtures/release-mini`, generated only by `evals/gen_corpus.py`) and reports tier routing accuracy, privacy/model-access enforcement, canary leaks, context-budget accounting, cross-process repeatability, and honest grep/stuff baselines. Thresholds in `evals/thresholds.toml` are digest-bound to the corpus, query set, and task set, so a stale, missing, or post-hoc-edited identity is refused instead of scored; CI now runs `bench run --repeat` plus `bench check` as a bounded offline gate.
- Adds the `experiment keygen|plan|validate|score|record` three-arm contract for no-wiki / current-wiki / updated-wiki conditions. Conditions map to blind labels via a keyed HMAC permutation of the frozen public identity under a host-private blinding key that `keygen` writes owner-only through the new `fsops.create_private_file` primitive; the grader packet carries no condition, key, or snapshot information, and `score` seals the blind per-label scores before reading the unblinding map. Scoring rejects cross-arm contamination, missing provenance, and malformed results, and returns typed `promoted`, `rollback-required`, or `unsettled` outcomes that `record` appends as leak-free audit events. Megamind plans, validates, scores, and records only - it never invokes a model, worker, network, or external service.
- Documents the surfaces and bumps the release to 0.5.0: new `docs/evaluation.md` and ADR 0009 (host-executed arms), evaluation contract sections in `docs/axi.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/schemas.md`, `docs/roadmap.md` (v0.5 with stated known limitations), `README.md`, and both copies of the skill `references/commands.md`, backed by `tests/test_evaluation.py` and new `fsops` coverage.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: Both round-5 findings are closed - the three stale doc copies now match the implemented unsettled-score ordering and the key write moved into `fsops.create_private_file` with its exclusive-0600-create, fsync, refuse-to-overwrite, and cleanup-on-failure semantics fully preserved and directly tested - and I re-verified for the branch as a whole that the frozen binding digests still match the fixture, query set, and task set, the skillpack copies are byte-identical, and the version is consistently 0.5.0, leaving only a documentation-sync nit.

## Testing

Installed the release wheel into a throwaway venv and drove both Phase 4 surfaces the way an end user would: the exact CI `bench run --repeat` / `bench check` pair passes all eight preregistered gates plus determinism with zero canary, budget, model-access, and contract violations, against grep and full-vault baselines that leak 6 and 4 canaries respectively; the three-arm contract runs keygen through record to a promoted outcome, and a no-improvement variant comes back typed rollback-required with a rollback reference. Twelve refusal paths (post-hoc thresholds, stale binding, missing gate, cross-arm contamination, raw snapshot digest, missing provenance, privacy violation, prompt leak, malformed accounting, both evidence-containment cases, incomplete arm set) all refuse with typed `evaluation_invalid` errors and leave no partial artifacts. A CPython audit hook armed against socket, DNS, HTTP, FTP, SMTP, and shell events recorded zero network events across the entire flow, with all 38 spawns being the public megamind preflight/route CLI. Targeted test files (evaluation, fsops, cli, examples, skillpack) all pass, and the worktree is clean. ## Summary

StructSplat shipped a `docs-sync` skill and a "docs updated in the same commit" definition-of-done, but had **no executable verification harness** — no docs↔code checker, no `verify.sh`, no CI, no registered pytest markers, and no central RNG seeding (across 100+ test files). This ports rtgs's engineering-discipline spine (**DOCS-003**), adapted to StructSplat's flat module layout and the NumPy/torch import split.

This is the **StructSplat half of a bidirectional infra transfer** with rtgs; the rtgs half (structure-tensor/WSE init, pooled row lifecycle, checkpoint policy, mask containment — all opt-in, tested) merged in intrinsicD/realtime-gs#13.

## What's in the spine

- **`scripts/docs_sync.py`** — torch-free, AST-based docs↔code checker: required docs exist, every skill is listed in `CLAUDE.md`, CLI subcommands + aliases are documented in README, every `init.STRATEGIES` entry is documented, `CLAUDE.md` path tokens resolve, and every `src/structsplat` module has a docstring. Exit 0 clean / 1 on drift.
- **`scripts/verify.sh`** — one CPU-only entry point: `ruff check` + `pytest -m "not slow and not integration"` + `docs_sync`.
- **`tests/conftest.py`** — autouse RNG seeding (NumPy always; torch only when importable, so a NumPy-only run never imports torch — preserves core invariant 1), and auto-marks the environment/evidence-coupled modules `integration`.
- **`pyproject.toml`** — registers `cuda`/`slow`/`integration` markers with `--strict-markers`; pins ruff lint to a correctness baseline (see below).
- **`tests/test_docs_sync.py`** — asserts the checker stays clean.
- **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`** — mirrors `verify.sh` on CPU (installs `.[dev,benchmark]`).
- **`README.md`** — documents the previously-undocumented `feedforward` strategy (drift the new checker surfaced).

## Two scoping decisions worth a reviewer's eye

**Lint baseline.** structsplat's `[tool.ruff]` pinned no `select`, so it silently inherited ruff 0.16's broad default ruleset — the tree carries **~1147 pre-existing style findings** (unsorted imports, blind-excepts, loop-var captures, …). Cleaning those is a repo-wide job, not this spine. I pinned an explicit **correctness baseline the whole tree already passes**: `select = ["E9", "F"]` (syntax errors + pyflakes: undefined names, unused imports). This also makes CI deterministic against ruff's shifting defaults. Broader style/import families and `ruff format --check` are deferred to a tracked DOCS-003 ratchet follow-up.

**Integration marker.** ~416 tests (the `ssp2e`/`ssp2v`/`ssp2f` actual-coder suites + evidence assays) need committed `results/` bundles (gitignored, absent from a fresh clone / CI runner), a Landlock-capable kernel, or a thread-pinned worker env. `conftest.py` auto-marks those modules `integration`; the default gate runs the portable subset. Run `-m integration` in a provisioned environment.

## Test plan / verification (local, CPU)

- `ruff check src tests scripts benchmarks` → **0 errors**
- `pytest -m "not slow and not integration"` → **1448 passed, 32 skipped, 416 deselected**
- `python scripts/docs_sync.py` → **OK**

Stage the style-lint ratchet: `ruff check --fix` the ~774 auto-fixable, triage the rest (B023 loop-var capture / BLE001 blind-except may be real), then widen the pinned `select` — and separately adopt `ruff format`.

labels.name: automation
labels.description: Work related to speeding up the development and testing processes

items.body:
Resolves #773

## Summary

Add support for S3 aws-chunked streaming uploads (`STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD`, `STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD-TRAILER`, `STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER`, and `Content-Encoding: aws-chunked` under `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD`) to the S3 gateway. The aws-chunked body is de-framed at the transport boundary so stored blobs, dedup, CRUSH placement, `getFile` hash verification, and splay/chain replication all use the *decoded* payload and its real content hash.

## What changed

- **`src/transport/aws_chunked.go`** (new): `awsChunkedReader` decodes the aws-chunked wire grammar (`<hex-size>[;chunk-signature=<64hex>]\r\n<raw data>\r\n` … terminating `0[;...]\r\n\r\n` + optional trailer block) with strict bounds — header lines ≤ 1 KiB, per-chunk size ≤ AWS 8 MiB cap, total decoded bytes capped at `common.MaxFileSize`. Computes the decoded SHA-256 and byte count on the stream.
- **Signed per-chunk verification**: each chunk is verified against the chained SigV4 streaming string-to-sign (`AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD\n<date>\n<scope>\n<prevSig>\n<emptySHA256>\n<hex(sha256(chunkData))>`) keyed by `deriveSigningKey` and seeded with the request signature. Reproduces the AWS documentation vector exactly (chunk sigs `ad80c7…`, `005562…`, `b6c6ea…`). The canonical header signature check keeps using the `STREAMING-*` literal as the payload hash, per the AWS spec.
- **`src/transport/s3_communicator.go`**: `HandshakeServer` detects streaming PUTs, derives the signing context from the verified request, emits `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` for `Expect: 100-continue`, sets a size-based read deadline, spills de-framed bytes to a bounded temp file, resolves `m.meta.Hash`/`m.meta.Size` to the decoded values (cross-checked against `X-Amz-Decoded-Content-Length`), and replays the spill through `S3Communicator.Read()`. Spill is closed/removed on every exit path. `ReceiveMetadata` (OPTIONS-handshake path) rejects `STREAMING-*` since it cannot authenticate chunk signatures.
- **Error mapping**: chunk signature mismatch → `403 SignatureDoesNotMatch`; malformed framing / decoded-length mismatch → `400 InvalidArgument`; oversized → `413 EntityTooLarge`.
- **Docs**: `docs/PROTOCOL.md` documents the streaming variants, de-framing, chunk signature algorithm, and the unsigned-streaming security posture.
- **Spec**: `openspec/changes/aws-chunked-streaming/` (proposal + spec + tasks).

## Test plan

- Unit tests reproduce the AWS documentation vector; corrupted signature, truncated chunk, missing terminator, unsigned trailer, oversized chunk, oversize total, header-line overflow.
- Gateway e2e: signed streaming PUT stores de-framed content with resolved `meta.Hash`/`meta.Size`; corrupted chunk signature → `EACCES`; `Expect: 100-continue`; decoded-length mismatch → `EBADMSG`; oversized → `413`; `STREAMING-*` on the handshake path rejected.
- Benchmarks: `BenchmarkAWSChunkedReaderSigned` (~89 MB/s) and `BenchmarkAWSChunkedReaderUnsigned` (~97 MB/s); results synced to `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` / `.github/data/benchmark_history.csv` by the pre-commit hook.
- `go vet`, `gofmt`, and all per-module test suites pass (`src` root, `common`, `transport`, `client`, `server`, `storage`, `metrics`, `crypto`, `p2p`).

## Changelog

- Added: aws-chunked streaming PUT support (signed and unsigned variants)
- Added: per-chunk SigV4 signature verification
- Added: `Expect: 100-continue` handling and size-based read deadlines for streaming bodies
- Added: spec `openspec/changes/aws-chunked-streaming/`
- Docs: `docs/PROTOCOL.md` S3 streaming section

items.title: Adopt Harbor-native regression-v1 math evaluation suite
items.body:
+## Problem

The benchmark surface was split across a large source catalog, acquisition and compiler code, custom agent runners, and A/B-specific cases. That made the v1 observation suite source-oriented and coupled to infrastructure that is not needed for task/verifier validation or a Jacobian workflow observation.

## Solution

- Replace the legacy benchmark surface with the committed Harbor `regression-v1` dataset containing eight self-contained mathematical tasks.
- Give each task schema 1.4 metadata, frozen offline input, an Oracle-only solution, a separate clean-room verifier, digest-bound evidence checks, and dimensioned rewards for correctness, evidence validity, scope accuracy, and assurance calibration.
- Remove the old catalog/compiler/handlers, custom `agent_ab` execution path, and their obsolete tests.
- Add Harbor Oracle and optional Jacobian observation job configurations with the authenticated `COMPUTE_VERIFY_NO_RETRIEVAL` sidecar boundary.
- Document that v1 is workflow observation only: it has no control arm or causal performance claim. The 18 public research challenges remain candidate material, and Lean/external proof backends stay out of this dataset until their runtimes are reliable.

## Testing

- `make check` — Ruff, formatting, mypy, and 299 unit tests passed.
- `make docs-linkcheck` — passed.
- `harbor sync benchmarks/regression-v1/dataset.toml` — all task digests current.
- `harbor run -c benchmarks/regression-v1/job-oracle.json --yes --quiet --n-concurrent 1 --jobs-dir benchmarks/results/regression-v1-oracle-final4` — 8/8 trials, zero exceptions, full reward.
- Failure probes covered empty output, wrong and incomplete claims, forged and symlinked evidence, and false `VERIFIED` assurance.

## Trust & Compatibility Impact

This changes benchmark and evaluation infrastructure only; it does not change Jacobian capability contracts, the verification kernel, or the public MCP API. The custom benchmark runner and source-oriented dataset are intentionally removed. No comparative performance claim is made by this PR.

items.title: Windowed concurrent ingest, compliance fixes, ops parity, and measured mainnet benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

This PR closes the performance and compliance gaps identified in the 2026-07-11 Go-vs-Rust review, in four commits:

1. **Windowed concurrent ingest with batched commits** (ADR 0020) — catch-up fetches up to `--ingest-window` blocks (default 64) with `--ingest-concurrency` concurrent node requests (default 8), committing each window in a single redb transaction; block parsing moves off the async runtime (`spawn_blocking`); locally computed txids are cross-checked against the node's verbose `getblock` list at fetch time and any divergence rejects the block loudly. Two ingestor bug fixes ride along: a node reporting a tip below the cached tip no longer drains the cache (rollback only on a genuine tip-hash disagreement), and a reorg reaching the `--start-height` floor empties the cache and resumes instead of wedging. Also in this commit, the RPC-compliance fixes vs the Go reference: `GetTreeState` by hash, pre-NU6.3 `GetSubtreeRoots` empty stream, `GetBlockRangeNullifiers` pool filtering, BIP34 `OP_1..OP_16` + genesis pseudo-height, the mempool staleness contract (ADR 0021: snapshots older than 60 s return `Unavailable` instead of serving stale data forever), `--zcash-conf` TOML-misconfig detection, and omitting `end: 0` in `getaddresstxids`.
2. **ADR audit** — all pre-existing ADRs re-checked against the code; 7 updated with supersession notes and cross-references.
3. **Ops-surface parity with Go** (ADR 0022) — gRPC reflection, `--log-level`/`--log-file` (JSON lines to file), Prometheus metrics default-on at `127.0.0.1:9068` (`--no-metrics` to disable), `--gen-cert-very-insecure`, darkside auto-shutdown (`--darkside-timeout-minutes`, default 30), `--nocache`, and `LWD_*` env fallbacks. The `./lightwalletd-rs-data` default data dir is kept as a documented divergence.
4. **Measured mainnet results** — README Performance section rewritten from real measurements against a fully synced mainnet zebrad v6.0.0 (snapshot-bootstrapped); the four read-path charts regenerated via `contrib/bench/scripts/plot.py`, plus a new ingest/full-sync chart. Curated results docs are committed under `contrib/bench/results/`.

## Headline measurements (details + caveats in the committed results docs)

- **Full genesis→tip mainnet sync: 1 h 22 m 30 s** (689 blocks/s overall, zero errors) vs the Go reference's extrapolated **≈9.5–10 h** (hit an 8-hour cap at 59.9%) — ~7× on identical hardware against the same node.
- Sandblasting-era ingest (start 1,780,000): **37.2 blocks/s** vs old-Rust 5.6 and Go 6.6.
- The fetch-time txid cross-check ran on every block of the full sync (~3.4 M blocks, v1–v5 txs) with zero mismatches.
- Read path unchanged-or-better: ~330k blocks/s `GetBlockRange` plateau on dense mainnet data; `GetBlock` p99 stays < 1.6 ms even while the ingestor runs flat out.
- Tuning: throughput in node-bound ranges scales to `--ingest-window 256 --ingest-concurrency 32` (~1.6× over the defaults through the spam era); defaults kept conservative.

## Testing

- `cargo test`: 234 lib tests + all integration suites green; `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` clean.
- New unit coverage: windowed ingest (whole-window commit, clamping, partial-window on fetch failure, mid-window reorg, node-behind idle/rollback, floor emptying), batch cache writes, txid cross-check, mempool staleness (paused-time), treestate-by-hash, nullifier pool filtering, BIP34 opcode heights, TOML misconfig, reflection (in-process).
- Runtime validation: full mainnet sync + three fixed-range ingest comparisons + the repo's own read-path harness, all against a real zebrad 6.0.0; no txid/hash mismatches, no reorg incidents.

## Notes for reviewers

- The behavioral divergences from Go are all deliberate and documented (CHANGELOG "RPC compliance" section + ADRs 0020–0022): where the reference is buggy (e.g. its treestate `SkipHash` walk is zcashd-only), the divergence is recorded instead of replicated.
- **Observable change at boot** (part of the ADR 0021 staleness contract): the mempool monitor's initial snapshot counts as maximally stale, so `GetMempoolTx`/`GetMempoolStream` return `Unavailable` between server start and the first successful mempool refresh (typically < 2 s), where they previously served an empty mempool. `Unavailable` is retryable by convention; a wallet connecting right at boot reconnects instead of briefly seeing a false empty mempool.
- Raw per-run benchmark outputs are git-ignored as before; only the two curated summary docs and the SVGs are committed.

items.title: Validate against real code, not just self-referential fixtures
items.body:
## Why

The repo's own dogfooding proved *consistency*, not *truth*: CI regenerates
`AGENTS.md` and fails on drift, but the only ground truth it compares against
is repoctx's own output. A scanner bug that silently drops a command would pass
CI with the file still wrong, and `audit --check` can never fail because the
file is regenerated right before it runs. Development was paused because the
tool had never been validated against real code — the thing the pause note
itself asked for.

This PR adds that validation so the project can keep being worked on with
evidence instead of vibes.

## What

- **Live-rot fixture + test** (`tests/fixtures/live/`, `TestAuditFlagsLiveRotInCLAUDE`): a hand-maintained `CLAUDE.md` containing real rot (ghost command + stale path). The audit must flag both and drop the score. This is the scenario the repo's own dogfooding can never produce.
- **Semantic self-assertion** (`TestSelfAGENTSKeepsCriticalFacts`): pins the facts `AGENTS.md` must never silently lose (`make test`, `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go.mod` module), so an adapter regression fails even when the generated diff looks plausible.
- **External-corpus benchmark** (`scripts/corpus.sh` + `testdata/corpus/` + CI `validation` job): clones four real repos at pinned SHAs (`spf13/cobra`, `expressjs/express`, `psf/black`, `rust-lang/rustlings`) and diffs extracted commands against **hand-reviewed golden files**. The golden files encode expected facts, not repoctx's own output — that's the anti-circularity break.
- **Dogfood rotation** (`scripts/dogfood.sh`): read-only runner against repositories you actually work on; first runs on two real projects are recorded in `docs/validation.md`.
- **Pause note removed** from the README, replaced by a pointer to `docs/validation.md`.

## Results worth reading

`docs/validation.md` records the first pass, including two findings the corpus surfaced that fixtures never would:

1. `info --json` emits `manifests[].commands: null` (not `[]`) for command-less manifests — indistinguishable from "extraction failed" per the frozen contract.
2. The scanner descends into test-data manifests (black's `tests/data/*/pyproject.toml`) and emits `pytest` for each — the main noise source on real repos.

Neither is changed here (contract is frozen post-1.0); they're documented as future-major work.

## Verification

- `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l .`, `go test ./...` all pass
- `repoctx generate .` is idempotent (AGENTS.md committed in sync)
- `make docs-examples` is idempotent
- `scripts/corpus.sh --fail` passes against all four pinned repos

items.title: fix(bench): measure the shipped retrieval path, not a copy of it
items.body:
## Why

`benchmarks/longmemeval/run.mjs` carried its own `CREATE TABLE`, its own FTS5 query construction and its own ranking. The published 95.40% R@5 scored **that reimplementation**, not MeMesh — and the two had drifted:

| | benchmark runner | shipped `search()` |
|---|---|---|
| query terms | OR-joined | space-joined = implicit **AND** |
| ordering | `ORDER BY rank` (BM25) | `ORDER BY e.id DESC` |

On the same 500 questions the runner reported **95.40%** and the product scored **5.20%**, with 473 of 500 returning nothing at all.

A benchmark that reimplements the thing it measures cannot fail when the thing breaks. Same shape as the hand-mirrored hook core PR #75 removed; same remedy — delete the copy.

## What changed

The runner seeds through `KnowledgeGraph.createEntity()` (the call `remember()` makes) and retrieves through `recallEnhanced()` (the call every transport makes). It records `run_info.measures: "shipped_recall_path"` so a result file states what produced it, sets `HOME` to a throwaway directory so a run cannot read the operator's config or write near their real knowledge graph, and fails with a readable message when `dist/` has not been built.

Modes now name real product configurations instead of adapter-internal fusion strategies: **A** without embeddings, **B** with them, populated through the product's own `embedAndStore()`. **Mode C is removed** — it applied a 60/40 weighted fusion MeMesh has never implemented, so there was no product behaviour for it to measure. Its historical result file is retained.

## Re-baselined numbers

| | R@5 | R@10 | MRR | zero-result questions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before the retrieval fixes | 5.20% | 5.20% | 0.0520 | 473 / 500 |
| **now (Mode A)** | **95.60%** | **97.80%** | **0.8931** | **0 / 500** |

**Mode B measures identical to Mode A, to every digit.** Populating embeddings changes nothing: `vectorSearch()` discards nearly every hit at `MAX_VECTOR_DISTANCE = 1` while sqlite-vec returns L2 distances around 1.2–1.4 for related text. The vector half of "hybrid search" contributes nothing today — a defect with its own fix pending. Its raw file is being regenerated because the run that produced these numbers started before the commit that rewrote the runner, so its `git_sha` points at the parent; a published result file has to agree with the code that produced it, which is this PR's whole subject.

Recomputed from the new raw file: 22 misses of 500 (4.4%), and **every one is a ranking failure, not a retrieval failure** — no question returned zero results, and 18 of the 22 had the right session in the returned set below position 5.

## Three published claims corrected, not quietly dropped

- **`RESULTS.md`** said the figure was "measured using FTS5 full-text search — the same retrieval engine MeMesh uses in production". It was not.
- **`METHODOLOGY.md` §3** concluded the benchmark was "a conservative lower bound on MeMesh's production retrieval quality — the full system would score at least as well, likely better". The 5.20% measurement disproved it in the most direct way available. The omissions §3 listed were real; the inference drawn from them was backwards, and that inference is what made the gap invisible — it told the reader the product was at least this good.
- **`METHODOLOGY.md` §4.2** listed OR-joining as an **adapter** limitation while the product AND-joined. The divergence was written down, in the published methodology, next to the number — and read as a caveat about the harness. §2.3 went further and documented the adapter's query builder in five numbered steps, a builder only the adapter had.

Result files from before the change are kept byte-identical — they are published evidence — and labelled in [`results/README.md`](benchmarks/longmemeval/results/README.md).

## New CI gate

`tests/recall-quality.test.ts`: ten memories, ten questions phrased the way a person asks them, thirty function-word notes so `limit: 5` has to choose which rows reach the scorer. Asserts an aggregate R@5 floor of 80% (measured 100%), on every CI leg. Synthetic on purpose — a 278 MB download per leg is unworkable and committing a dataset slice is redistribution.

Break matrix, each edit grep-confirmed then reverted:

| break | R@5 | gate |
|---|---|---|
| AND-joined query terms | 0% | **fails** |
| `ORDER BY e.id DESC` before `LIMIT` | 20% | **fails** |
| flat relevance value | 100% | passes |
| whitespace tokenising | 90% | passes |

The previous commit claimed all four breach it. They do not, and the claim is corrected in this PR rather than left standing. The first two are collapse-class; the last two cost individual terms and positions, and tuning the corpus until they breach an aggregate floor would mean contriving questions where every distinctive term carries punctuation. They are pinned by the targeted cases in `tests/recall-relevance.test.ts` instead. The split is recorded in the gate's own docstring, along with two properties it deliberately does not assert and why.

## Incidental

`.gitignore` excluded `benchmarks/` outright. Git does not descend into an excluded directory, so the two `!benchmarks/longmemeval/**` exceptions below it never took effect and a new file in the published evidence pack could not be added without `-f`. Changed to `benchmarks/*`.

## Verification

```
npm test -- --run        76 files / 1187 tests passed, 0 failures
npm run typecheck        clean
npm run lint             clean (--max-warnings 0)
npm run build            6/6 smoke tests passed
run.mjs --mode A         R@5 95.60%  R@10 97.80%  MRR 0.8931  zero-result 0/500  9.5s
run.mjs --mode B         R@5 95.60%  R@10 97.80%  MRR 0.8931  (identical to A)
```

## Docs synced

- [x] CHANGELOG.md updated for the change
- [ ] docs/ARCHITECTURE.md — N/A, no module or dependency change
- [ ] docs/api/API_REFERENCE.md — N/A, no HTTP/CLI/MCP surface change
- [ ] README.md — N/A. The README's headline figure is a separate decision and this PR touches no published claim outside `benchmarks/`. Note it currently reads 95.40%; the measured figure is now 95.60%.
- [ ] README locales — N/A, README unchanged
- [x] Benchmark docs (RESULTS / METHODOLOGY / REPRODUCE / results/README) rewritten to describe what the runner now measures
- [ ] Version files — N/A, no version bump
- [x] dist/ unchanged by this PR (no `src/` change); `dist/skills-manifest.json` untouched
- [x] Reviewer brief includes doc-sync verification

Consolidates the `audit/scientific-hardening` work into `main`.

## What this branch establishes

**Honest narrowing (map recovery).** Comparative epistasis-map-recovery claims are retracted:
compressed-sensing, isotropic and pairwise-targeted D-optimal acquisition, and correlated-error
inference all show map recovery is weak/confounded and order-3 is out of budget at B<=192 — the ESM
prior, not the acquisition geometry, carries the weak pairwise signal. README and `docs/VALIDATION.md`
narrowed; the claim registry synced.

**Downstream-impact benchmark (the positive result).** At equal budget, a structure-aware plate is a
better training set for ranking held-out double/triple mutants than fitness-greedy and random:

- **GB1 — decision-eligible:** structural beats fitness 20/20 (S_macro-AUC +0.342) and random (+0.175);
  the ESM masking-variance prior adds nothing (info vs structural not supported).
- **TrpB (Johnston 2024; enzyme catalysis, independent of GB1's binding assay) — exploratory
  replication:** structural beats random and fitness 20/20 (+0.135, +0.286). Non-decision-eligible
  (scored at `n_perturbations=0` to fit a compute budget; the info method is degenerate there and not
  claimed).

**Robustness controls.** A permutation null collapses structural−random from +0.175 to +0.0046 (GB1)
and +0.135 to +0.0135 (TrpB) — genuine epistatic-learning signal, not a coverage artifact (a small
coverage residual, ~3% / ~10%, is disclosed). The benchmark is deterministic.

**Engineering.** The downstream CLI is dataset-generic (`--dataset`, `--n-perturbations`); the
confirmatory profile pins the scoring recipe so a non-standard cache is honestly non-decision-eligible.
